title: How people read it
hook: it takes around ninety minutes; many read one ashtpadi a day
tomorrow: Ashtpadi 1, salok: I bow to the Guru

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sukhmani, and your line: the jewel of peace. Did you picture the jewel in the middle of something hard? Today, how people actually read a bani this long. Day four hundred thirty-seven.

Sukhmani is long. Read aloud at an unhurried pace, it fills a good stretch of a morning. So how does anyone with a job, children and a commute read it at all? A grandmother up before dawn may read the whole of it, every day. A nurse on night shifts may not have that much quiet time in a whole week. And yet both of them can call Sukhmani their bani. The answer isn't a trick. It's in how the text was built, eight stanzas at a time.
screen: `A LONG BANI, A SHORT MORNING.` → `A GRANDMOTHER AND A NURSE.` → `THE ANSWER IS IN THE STRUCTURE.`

segments.voice: Sukhmani is made of twenty-four ashtpadis. Asht is eight; pad is a stanza or verse. So an ashtpadi is an eight-stanza section. Each one opens with a short salok, two lines that set the theme, and then the eight stanzas unfold it. Twenty-four times eight is one hundred ninety-two stanzas in all. That structure is a gift to a busy person. An ashtpadi is a complete thought. It has a beginning, a middle and an end. You can read one in a few minutes and close the book having heard something whole. So people read Sukhmani in many ways. Some read all of it every day, often early in the morning. Some read it through once a week. Families and groups sometimes split it up, a few ashtpadis each, so that together they complete it. And some read just one ashtpadi a day, so that the whole bani comes round in twenty-four days. Sikh tradition doesn't set one required pace for Sukhmani. What matters, in the bani's own words, is that the Name rests in the mind. A rushed reading of all twenty-four is not the goal. An attentive reading of one is a real reading. That's the pace we'll take on this path: one ashtpadi at a time, its salok first, then a few days with its stanzas, then a day for living it.
screen: `ASHT: EIGHT. PAD: A STANZA.` · `A SALOK, THEN EIGHT STANZAS.` · `ALL AT ONCE, OR ONE A DAY.` · `ATTENTION OVER SPEED.` · then, large: `ONE ASHTPADI AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan an ashtpadi a week. Think about your actual week, not an ideal one. Where is there a quiet ten minutes? Sunday morning before anyone's up. A lunch break in the car. The bus home on Wednesday. Pick one slot and picture yourself there, a book or a phone in your hand, reading eight stanzas slowly. Then let the plan go and just breathe for a little while, as if that slot had already arrived. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once. The bell holds the time.
How people read it. Sukhmani's twenty-four ashtpadis, each a salok and eight stanzas, read all at once, shared among a group, or one at a time.
Your line: one ashtpadi at a time. Today, put the slot you chose into your calendar, with a reminder, so the plan has somewhere to live. Day four hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Some Sikhs read the whole of Sukhmani Sahib daily or weekly; others read one ashtpadi a day, and families and groups sometimes divide the twenty-four ashtpadis among themselves to complete it together.
